en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Inference: 1.
The Question on Inference
Then King Milinda approached the Venerable Nāgasena; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Nāgasena and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, King Milinda—desiring to know, desiring to hear, desiring to retain [the teaching], desiring to see the light of knowledge, desiring to shatter ignorance, and desiring to produce the light of knowledge—[addressed him].
Desiring to destroy the darkness of ignorance, and having established exceptional fortitude, energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension,
he said this to the Venerable Nāgasena:
“Venerable Nāgasena, have you ever seen the Buddha?”
“No indeed, Great King.
“But have you seen the Buddha with your teachers?
“No indeed, Great King.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, it is said that you have not seen the Buddha, nor has the Buddha been seen by your teachers.
Therefore, venerable Nāgasena, the Buddha does not exist; for here the Buddha is not perceived.
“But, Great King, do you have ancestors among the Kṣatriyas who were the forebears of your royal lineage?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
Of course there is no doubt; there were ancient kṣatriyas who were the predecessors of my kṣatriya lineage.
“Have you ever seen those ancient kṣatriyas before, Great King?”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“But, Great King, have you ever seen those former khattiyas who instructed you—the chaplains, the generals, the judges, and the high ministers?
“No indeed, Bhante.”

“But if, Great King, you have not seen those ancient Kṣatriyas, nor indeed have your instructors seen those ancient Kṣatriyas, then there are no ancient Kṣatriyas, for no ancient Kṣatriyas are known here.
“Venerable Nāgasena, the articles of enjoyment and possessions used by the ancient Kṣatriyas are seen.
That is to say:”
“The white parasol, the turban, the sandals, the yak-tail fan, the sword-jewel, and the magnificent couches—
by these we would know and believe that there were former kṣatriyas.
“In just this way, great king, we too would know and believe in this Blessed One.”
"There is that reason by which we might know and believe: 'That Blessed One exists.
What is that reason?
Great King, there are indeed articles of personal use experienced by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
That is to say: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— by means of these, the world with its devas knows and has faith.
‘That Blessed One exists.
By this reason, O Great King, by this cause, by this method, and by this inference, it should be known that ‘that Blessed One exists.
‘Having ferried across many people, ...’
“Extinguished through the destruction of the acquisitions;
by inference it should be known that he,
the supreme among bipeds, exists.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, please provide a simile.
“Just as if, O Great King, a city-builder desiring to construct a city were first to survey a level piece of ground—
neither rising nor falling, free from gravel and stones, secure, blameless, and delightful— and having found such a site there...”

Having leveled that uneven ground and cleared it of stumps and thorns, he would build there a beautiful city—well-planned, measured out in sections, with moats and walls dug deep, and equipped with strong gate-towers, watchtowers, and battlements; featuring many crossroads, four-way junctions, and intersections;
with clean, level royal highways and well-arranged market stalls; and endowed with parks, gardens, ponds, lotus pools, and wells.
Adorned with many kinds of divine dwellings and free from all defects, suppose that city, having reached full development in every respect,
were to move to another region; then, at a later time, that city would become prosperous,
flourishing, well-supplied with food, secure, successful, auspicious, free from calamity, free from distress, and crowded with various people.
There were many khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas; elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, and infantrymen;
archers, javelin-men, standard-bearers, and flag-bearers; alms-givers, nobles, princes, and high-born youths; brave men, mighty warriors, heroes, shield-bearers, and combatants;
sons of slaves, sons of hired servants, wrestlers, accountants, cooks, chefs, barbers, bath-attendants, and tailors.
Gardeners, goldsmiths, bellows-makers, lead-workers, tin-workers, ironworkers, lathe-workers, smiths, jewelers,
weavers, potters, basket-makers, salt-makers, leather-workers, chariot-makers, ivory-workers, rope-makers,
mattress-makers, thread-spinners, blowpipe-makers, bow-makers, bowstring-makers, fletchers, painters, dyers, and washermen; as well as weavers.
Tailors, coin-examiners, cloth-dealers, perfumers, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, hired laborers, leaf-sellers, fruit-sellers,
root-sellers, rice-sellers, cake-sellers, fish-sellers, meat-sellers, liquor-sellers, actors, dancers, acrobats, illusionists, corpse-burners, wrestlers,
corpse-removers, bamboo-workers, hunters, courtesans, female dancers, and water-carriers.
People from various regions— those from Sāketa, Vana, Cīna, Vilāta, Ujjenī, Bhārukaccha, Kāsi-Kosala, Pāraṃtaka,
Māgadha, Sāketa, Soreyya, Pāvā, Koṭumbara-Mathurā, Alasanda, Kaśmīra, and Gandhāra— had come to that city for residence;
they beheld that city, which was new, well-laid out, faultless, blameless, and delightful.
Having seen it, they know by inference: "Ah, truly skilled is that city-builder who constructed this city!

In the same way, Great King, that Blessed One is peerless, equal to the unequaled, without rival, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, unfathomable, possessed of infinite virtues, having reached the perfection of qualities, with infinite steadfastness, infinite majesty, and infinite energy.
Possessing infinite power and having reached the perfection of the Buddha’s strength, he defeated Māra together with his army, tore asunder the net of views, exhausted ignorance,
and gave rise to true knowledge. Having borne the torch of the Dhamma and attained omniscience,
he— having won the battle— founded the City of Dhamma.
Great King, the City of Dhamma belonging to the Blessed One has virtue as its rampart,

modesty as its moat, knowledge as its gateway-tower, energy as its watchtowers, faith as its main pillar, mindfulness as its gatekeeper, wisdom as its palace, the Suttantas as its crossroads, the Abhidhamma as its central square,
the Vinaya as its judicial hall, and the Foundations of Mindfulness as its street. And within that street of the Foundations of Mindfulness, Great King—
Such shops were set out there, namely: a flower shop,
a perfume shop, a fruit shop, an antidote shop, a medicine shop, an ambrosia shop, a jewel shop, and a general goods shop.
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the ‘flower shop’ of the Blessed Buddha?
“There is, Great King, a classification of objects of focus (ārammaṇa-vibhatti) explained by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Namely as follows:”
The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of relinquishment,

the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of disenchantment with the entire world, the perception of impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, mindfulness of breathing, the perception of a bloated corpse,
the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, and the perception of a scattered corpse.

The perception of the slain and scattered, the perception of the bloody, the perception of the festering, the perception of the skeletal, the perception of loving-kindness, the perception of compassion,
the perception of sympathetic joy, the perception of equanimity, the recollection of death, and mindfulness directed to the body— these, O Great King,
are the classifications of objects taught by the Blessed Buddha.
In this regard, whoever desires to be liberated from aging and death takes up one or another of those objects as a mental support.
By means of that object, he is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion, liberated from conceit, and liberated from wrong views;
he crosses over saṃsāra, stops the stream of craving, purifies the threefold stain, and [abandons] all defilements.
Having struck down [the defilements] and entered the supreme city of Nibbāna— which is stainless, dustless, pure, bright, unborn, undecaying,
deathless, blissful, cooled, and fearless— he liberates his mind in Arahatship; this, O Great King, is called ‘The Blessed One’s Flower Shop.’
"Having taken up the root of action,
go to the marketplace;
having purchased an object, [proceed]."
“Therefore, be released by means of liberation.
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the perfume shop of the Blessed Buddha?
“There is, Great King, a classification of virtues taught by that Blessed One; by the fragrance of that virtue—”
Anointed with this, the sons of the Blessed One perfume and thoroughly suffuse the world with its devas with the fragrance of their virtue;
they waft and blow forth in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, with the wind and against the wind, pervading all and remaining there.
What are those classifications of virtue?
The virtue of taking refuge, the fivefold virtue, the eightfold virtue, the tenfold virtue, and the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha included in the five recitations—
this, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s perfume shop.
And this, O Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God above gods:
‘The scent of flowers does not go against the wind,
nor do sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine;
but the fragrance of the virtuous goes even against the wind.
The person of noble character wafts his fragrance in all directions—
whether it be sandalwood or tagara,
or the blue lotus or the jasmine.
Of all these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
This fragrance is not of the earth; it is subtle.
“The fragrance of tagara and sandalwood,
however excellent it may be, does not compare to the supreme fragrance of those possessed of virtue,
which wafts even among the gods.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the Buddha, the Blessed One’s ‘marketplace of fruits’?
“The fruits, great king, have been declared by the Blessed One.
They are as follows:”

The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arahantship, the attainment of the fruit of emptiness, the attainment of the fruit of the signless, and the attainment of the fruit of the desireless. In this regard,
whoever desires any such fruit gives the root of kamma and purchases the desired fruit—

whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arahantship, the attainment of the fruit of emptiness, the attainment of the fruit of the signless, or the attainment of the fruit of the desireless.
It is just as if, Great King, there were a mango tree with constant fruit belonging to a certain man;
he would not pluck the fruits from it until the tax-collectors arrived. But when the tax-collectors had arrived, having taken hold of the root, he would point it out thus:
"O man, this is indeed a mango tree with constant fruit; take from it as much fruit as you desire."
‘Whether it be a *salāṭuka*, a *dovila*, or a *kesika*—whether raw or cooked.
Then, according to the price he himself has paid, if he desires a *salāṭuka*, he takes a *salāṭuka*; if he desires a *dovila*, he takes a *dovila*;
if he desires a *kesika*, he takes a *kesika*; if he desires something raw, he takes something raw; if...
He desires what is ripe; he takes what is ripe.
In the same way, Great King, whoever desires whatever fruit, having given the root of karma, takes the desired fruit—whether it be the fruit of stream-entry...
or even the attainment of the fruit of the wishless. This, Great King, is called “the Blessed One’s fruit-shop.”
“Having given what is rooted in kamma,
people reap the fruit of the Deathless;
by that they become happy.”
“...those worms which have the fruit of immortality.
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the medicine shop of the Blessed Buddha?
“The medicines, Great King, were explained by the Blessed One—by means of those medicines the Blessed One delivers the world with its devas from the poison of the defilements.”
"But what, Great King, are those antidotes?
They are these four noble truths proclaimed by the Blessed One.
That is to say:"
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering— therein,
whoever seeks higher knowledge and hears this Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths is liberated from birth,
liberated from aging, liberated from death, and liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They are completely liberated; this, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s pharmacy.
‘Whatever antidotes exist in the world that ward off poisons, [they are all surpassed by this].’”
“There is nothing equal to the medicine of the Dhamma;
drink this, O bhikkhus.
“Venerable Nāgasena, what was the Blessed Buddha’s pharmacy?”
“Medicines, Great King, have been declared by the Blessed One—those medicines with which the Blessed One heals gods and humans. Namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, and the five faculties.”
The seven powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— by means of these medicines,
the Blessed One purges wrong view, purges wrong intention, purges wrong speech, purges wrong action,
purges wrong livelihood, purges wrong effort, purges wrong mindfulness, and purges wrong concentration.

It purges greed, causes the vomiting of greed; it causes the vomiting of hatred, causes the vomiting of delusion, causes the vomiting of conceit, causes the vomiting of wrong views, causes the vomiting of doubt, causes the vomiting of restlessness, causes the vomiting of sloth and torpor, causes the vomiting of shamelessness and lack of moral dread, and causes the vomiting of all defilements. This, O Great King, is what is called...
“The Blessed One’s medicine shop.
“Whatever various and many medicines exist in the world;”
There is nothing equal to the medicine of the Dhamma;
drink this, O bhikkhus.
Having drunk the medicine of the Dhamma, [you shall be free from suffering].
"May they be free from aging and death;
having cultivated [the path] and seen [the truth],
may they be extinguished through the destruction of the acquisitions."
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the ‘Ambrosial Shop’ of the Blessed Buddha?
“The Ambrosia, Great King, has been proclaimed by the Blessed One; with that Ambrosia the Blessed One sprinkled the world together with its devas.
Sprinkled with that Ambrosia, gods and humans were liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
What is that deathless? It is this:
mindfulness directed to the body.
This too, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods: “Those, bhikkhus, who partake of mindfulness directed to the body partake of the deathless.”
This, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s Pharmacy of the Deathless.
Having seen the people afflicted by disease,
he opened the pharmacy of the deathless.
“Having purchased it with kamma,
O bhikkhus, take hold of the Deathless!
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the Blessed Buddha’s jewel-mall?”

“Indeed, Great King, treasures have been proclaimed by the Blessed One, and adorned with these treasures, the sons of the Blessed One illuminate, radiate, shine, glow, and blaze forth throughout the world including its devas; they display light above, below, and across.
What are those treasures?

The jewel of virtue, the jewel of concentration, the jewel of wisdom, the jewel of liberation, the jewel of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the jewel of the analytical knowledges, and the jewel of the factors of enlightenment.
And what, Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of virtue?

It is the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, the virtue of purity of livelihood, the virtue concerning the requisites, the minor virtue, the intermediate virtue, the major virtue, the virtue of the path, and the virtue of the fruit.
Great King, the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās,
and this generation with its recluses and brahmins, yearns for and aspires to a person adorned with the jewel of virtue. Great King, a bhikkhu who is bedecked with the jewel of virtue shines forth,
shines exceedingly— toward the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, above, below, and across— down as far as the Avīci hell.
From the peak of existence above down to this point, it stands surpassing, excelling, and overwhelming all other jewels.
Such, O Great King, are the jewels of virtue displayed in the Blessed One’s jewel-market;
this, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s jewel of virtue.’
“Such virtues as these are in the Buddha’s shop;
having purchased them with one’s own karma,”
“‘Put on the jewel!
What, Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of concentration?

It is concentration with directed thought and evaluation; concentration without directed thought and with only evaluation; concentration without directed thought and without evaluation; emptiness concentration; signless concentration; and desireless concentration.”
“Great King, when a bhikkhu wears the jewel of concentration, all those thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty; pride, restlessness, views, and doubt;
the bases of the defilements, and various evil thoughts—all these, upon encountering concentration, scatter, disperse, and fall apart;
they do not remain and do not adhere.”
Just as, Great King, water scattered upon a lotus leaf disperses, vanishes, falls apart, does not remain,
and does not adhere— why is that? Because of the purity of the lotus.

In the same way, Great King, for a bhikkhu who has donned the jewel of concentration, whatever thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty there may be, as well as pride, restlessness, views, doubt,
the bases of the defilements, and various other evil thoughts— all these, upon encountering concentration, scatter, disperse, and fall apart;
they do not remain stable and do not adhere.
And for what reason?
Because of the utter purity of his concentration.
This, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s jewel of concentration. Such, O Great King, are the jewels of concentration displayed in the Blessed One’s jeweled shop.
“In one who wears the garland of the jewel of concentration,
unwholesome thoughts do not arise,
nor does the mind waver.”
“Adorn yourselves with this!
“And what, Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of wisdom?
It is that wisdom, Great King, by which a noble disciple understands, as it truly is: ‘This is wholesome,’ and ‘This is...”
He understands as it really is: "This is unwholesome"; he understands as it really is: "This is blameworthy, this is blameless;
this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated; this is inferior, this is superior; this is dark, this is bright;
this is the counterpart of both the dark and the bright. He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."

He understands it as it truly is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ he understands it as it truly is; ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ he understands it as it truly is.
This, Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s jewel of wisdom.’
“For one who wears the garland of the jewel of wisdom,
existence does not endure for long;
swiftly he touches the Deathless.”
"And that existence does not please him.
"And what, Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of liberation?
The jewel of liberation, Great King, is said to be arahantship. A bhikkhu who has attained arahantship, Great King, is said to be 'adorned with the jewel of liberation.'"
Just as, Great King, a man adorned with ornaments of pearl clusters, gem clusters, and coral clusters, his body anointed with agallochum,
tagara, tālīsa, and red sandalwood, and variegated with nāga, punnāga, sāla, salaḷa, campaka, yūthikā, atimuttaka, pāṭali, blue lotus, vassikī, and mallikā flowers,
would outshine all other people and shine, shine exceedingly, radiate, illuminate, illuminate thoroughly, blaze, and glow intensely.
It surpasses and overwhelms them with its garlands,
perfumes, jewels, and ornaments. In the same way, Great King, one who has attained arahantship, whose taints are destroyed,
and who is adorned with the jewel of liberation, outshines and excels all other monks who are liberated, surpassing them and transcending them, shining forth, radiating splendor.
It shines, blazes, and glows; it overpowers and overspreads with liberation.
For what reason?
Because, Great King, this is the foremost of all ornaments, namely, the ornament of liberation.
This, O Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s jewel of liberation.
‘The people look up to their master, who wears a garland of jewels in his house;’
“The world together with its devas gazes upon the garland of the jewel of liberation. And what,
Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of the knowledge and vision of liberation?

“Great King, the knowledge of reviewing is called the Blessed One’s jewel of the knowledge and vision of liberation. By means of that knowledge, the noble disciple reviews the paths, fruits, and nibbāna, as well as the defilements already abandoned and those remaining to be abandoned.
It is by means of this knowledge that the noble ones awaken to the state of having fulfilled their task.”
"O sons of the Conqueror, strive to obtain that jewel of knowledge! "And what,
Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā)?"

There are, O Great King, four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*): the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*nirutti*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

Adorned, O Great King, with these four jewels of analytical knowledge, whatever assembly a bhikkhu approaches—whether an assembly of kshatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, or an assembly of householders—[he enters it with confidence].
Confident, he approaches the assembly of recluses; undaunted, fearless, untroubled, without terror, and with his hair standing on end gone, he approaches the assembly.
Great King, it is just as a warrior, a hero in battle, equipped with his five weapons, enters the fray without fear.
‘If my enemies are far off, I will strike them down with an arrow; if they are closer than that, I will strike them with a spear;
if they are closer than that, I will strike them with a javelin; when they have come near, I will cut them in two with a discus;
when they have reached my body, I will pierce them through with a dagger.’
In the same way, Great King, a bhikkhu adorned with the jewel of the four analytical knowledges approaches an assembly without fear, thinking:
"Whoever shall ask me a question regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning, I will explain meaning by means of meaning;
I will explain cause by means of cause; I will explain reason by means of reason; I will explain method by means of method."
I shall act without doubt; I shall dispel uncertainty; I shall satisfy [him] with the answer to his question.

Whatever person asks me a question regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), I will explain phenomenon by means of phenomenon, explain the deathless by means of the deathless, explain the unconditioned by means of the unconditioned, and explain Nibbāna by means of Nibbāna.

I shall speak; I shall speak of emptiness by means of emptiness, I shall speak of the signless by means of the signless, I shall speak of the wishless by means of the wishless, I shall speak of the unshakable by means of the unshakable.
I shall bring about certainty, I shall dispel doubt, and I shall satisfy you with the answering of your question.
Whoever shall ask me a question regarding the analytical knowledge of language, to him I shall explain language by means of language;
I shall explain word by word, phrase by phrase, syllable by syllable, euphonic combination by euphonic combination, phoneme by phoneme, and secondary phoneme by secondary phoneme.
I shall speak; I shall speak praise with praise, tone with tone, designation with designation, and conventional usage with conventional usage.
I shall remove doubt, dispel perplexity, and satisfy you with my answer to your question.
‘Whoever asks me a question regarding the analytical knowledge of ready wit, I shall answer with ready wit;
I shall explain with a simile; I shall explain with a characteristic mark; I shall explain with a flavor;
I shall remove doubt; I shall dispel uncertainty; I shall satisfy them with my explanation of the question.’”
This, O Great King, is called ‘the Jewel of the Analytical Knowledges of the Blessed One.
“Whoever, having purchased the analytical knowledges, should touch them with wisdom;”
“Unafraid and undaunted,
he outshines the world with its devas.
And what, Great King, is the Blessed One’s jewel of the factors of enlightenment?

“Great King, there are these seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment.

Adorned with these seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment, Great King, a bhikkhu overcomes all darkness and illuminates, radiates light upon, and generates luminosity throughout the world together with its devas.
This, Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s jewel of the factors of enlightenment.’”
“Devas and humans alike arise for the sake of the garland of the jewels of the factors of enlightenment;
having purchased that through kamma,”
“Put on this jewel as an ornament.
“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the ‘all-shops’ of the Blessed Buddha?
“The ‘all-shops,’ O Great King, of the Blessed One consists of the ninefold word of the Buddha, the bodily relics, the objects used by him, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.”
In the market of all things, O Great King, the Blessed One has displayed the perfection of birth,
displayed the perfection of wealth, displayed the perfection of longevity, displayed the perfection of health, displayed the perfection of beauty,
displayed the perfection of wisdom, displayed the perfection of human excellence, displayed the perfection of divine excellence, and displayed the perfection of Nibbāna.
In this regard, those who desire various forms of success purchase that success—whatever they have prayed for—by paying the price of karma;
some purchase it by undertaking moral discipline (*sīla*), and some purchase it by the performance of the Uposatha observance.
Even with a small amount of the price of karma, they obtain success again and again.

“Just as, Great King, in a merchant’s shop, people take sesame, mung beans, and black gram by taking little by little—even with a small amount of rice, mung beans, or black gram—and pay for them at a low price;
even so, Great King, in the Blessed One’s universal shop, beings obtain successes by taking little by little, even through the small root-cause of their karma.
This, Great King, is called ‘the Blessed One’s universal shop.’”
Long life, health, beauty,
heaven, birth in a high family,
And the unconditioned, the deathless.
In the Victor’s universal marketplace,
one acquires [the fruit] by means of karma as the capital, whether it be small or great.
“Having purchased [the path] with the root of faith,
may you, O bhikkhus, be successful!
Such people as these, O Great King, dwell in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma— namely, those versed in the Suttas and those versed in the Vinaya.

They were experts in the Abhidhamma, preachers of the Dhamma, reciters of the Jātakas, reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya, reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya;
they were endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom;

they delighted in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, were practitioners of insight, devoted to their own welfare, forest-dwellers, dwellers at the foot of trees, dwellers in the open air, dwellers on heaps of straw, and dwellers in cemeteries.

The city of Dhamma was crowded, thronged, filled, and completely packed with those practicing the perpetual sitter’s vow, those established in the fruits, those in training (sekha), those possessing the fruits—namely, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants;
those possessing the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and supernormal powers; those who have reached perfection in wisdom;

those skilled in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble paths, the jhānas, the liberations, and the peaceful attainments of the form and formless realms—with those arahants it was as if the city were a dense thicket of reeds and cane.
It is said here:
"Free from passion, free from hatred,
free from delusion, and without taints;"
Free from craving and without grasping,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma;
forest-dwellers who uphold the ascetic practices.
Meditating with coarse robes,
the wise who delight in seclusion dwell in the city of Dhamma.
Those who never lie down, those who use only mats,
as well as those who stand or walk in meditation;
all of them wear robes made of discarded rags.
They dwell in the City of Dhamma,
wearing the three robes,
with a piece of hide as their fourth.
Delighting in a single seat,
those wise ones dwell in the City of Dhamma—
those of few desires, prudent, and steadfast.
Eating little and free from greed,
content with gain or loss,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma.
The wise ones who meditate, delighting in jhāna,
with peaceful minds and concentrated,
aspire to the state of nothingness.
They dwell in the City of Dhamma:
those practicing the path and those established in the fruits,
the trainees who possess the fruits.
Aspiring for the supreme goal,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma;
the stainless ones who have entered the stream.
Those who are once-returners,
non-returners, and arhats—
they dwell in the City of Dhamma.
Skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,
delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment,
practitioners of insight, and upholders of the Dhamma—
They dwell in the city of Dhamma,
skilled in the bases of psychic power and delighting in the cultivation of concentration.
Devoted to the right efforts,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma;
having attained perfection in direct knowledge, they abide there.
Delighting in their own domain,
moving through the atmosphere,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma.
With downcast eyes, speaking in moderation,
guarding the doors of the senses and well-restrained,
they are well-tamed in the highest taming.
They dwell in the City of Dhamma—
possessors of the three knowledges and the six superknowledges,
who have reached perfection in spiritual power.
“Having reached perfection in wisdom,
they dwell in the City of Dhamma.
Those monks, O Great King, who possess the supreme treasure of immeasurable knowledge, are unattached, of incomparable virtue, incomparable fame, and incomparable power.
"O Great King, those bhikkhus who possess incomparable splendor, who have set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, and who have reached the perfection of wisdom— such as these, O Great King,
are called the 'Generals of the Dhamma' in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
Furthermore, O Great King, those bhikkhus who possess supernormal powers, who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), who have achieved fearlessness, and who move through the sky— "
Difficult to approach, difficult to overcome, moving without a fixed support, capable of shaking the earth together with its oceans, mountains, and pathways, able to rub the sun and moon,
skilled in the manifestation of transformations and resolutions, and having reached perfection in psychic power— such, O Great King,
are the bhikkhus who are called the "chaplain" in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
But those monks, O Great King, who follow the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), who have few desires, are contented, and loathe soliciting or seeking [alms],
who wander for alms from house to house in regular succession like bees entering a secluded forest after savoring the fragrance,
who are indifferent to both body and life, who have attained Arahantship, and who are ranked foremost in the virtues of the ascetic practices— such as these, O Great King, [are the monks].
Great King, in the Blessed One’s city of Dhamma, the bhikkhus are called ‘gamblers. But those bhikkhus, Great King,
who are utterly pure, stainless, free from defilements, skilled in passing away and reappearing,
and have reached perfection in the divine eye— such bhikkhus, Great King, are called ‘illuminators of the city’ in the Blessed One’s city of Dhamma.
But those monks, O Great King, who are learned, who have mastered the traditional scriptures, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā;
who are skilled in the distinctions between lax and tense, long and short, heavy and light syllables;
who are bearers of the ninefold teaching—such monks, O Great King, are called the "Guardians of the Dhamma" in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.

Furthermore, Great King, those bhikkhus who are knowers of the Vinaya, experts in the Vinaya, skilled in what is possible and what is impossible; who are proficient in offenses and non-offenses, heavy and light offenses, those that can be remedied and those that cannot, as well as in restoration, confession, censure, atonement, rehabilitation, suspension, and reconciliation;
who have reached perfection in the Vinaya—such bhikkhus, Great King, are called the ‘guardians of the walls’ in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.

Furthermore, Great King, those bhikkhus who are adorned with the garlands of the flowers of supreme liberation, and who have attained the state that is most excellent, sublime, precious, and foremost—
"O Great King, such bhikkhus as these— who are beloved and longed for by the many— are called 'flower-sellers' in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
But those bhikkhus, O Great King, who have penetrated the realization of the Four Noble Truths, who have seen the Truth and understood the Teaching,"
"Having crossed over doubt regarding the four fruits of recluseship and having attained the bliss of those fruits, they share those fruits with others who are practicing the path.
Such monks, O Great King, are called 'fruit-sellers' in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
Furthermore, O Great King, those monks who are anointed with the perfume of the restraint of virtue and who possess manifold and abundant qualities..."
"O Great King, those bhikkhus who dispel the foul odor of the stains of defilement— such as these, O Great King, are called 'perfume-sellers' in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
Furthermore, O Great King, those bhikkhus who desire the Dhamma, who delight in its proclamation, and who possess sublime joy in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya..."
Whether they have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, they drink the supreme flavor of the Dhamma; having plunged into the supreme flavor of the Dhamma with body,
speech, and mind, they possess extraordinary eloquence, are engaged in the search for the Dhamma among all teachings,
and wherever there may be— here or there— a discourse on fewness of desires, on contentment, on seclusion, or on non-association.
Discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation—
having gone here and there, they drink that particular flavor of discourse. It is such monks, O Great King,
who are called ‘the thirsty gluttons’ in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
But those monks, O Great King, who are devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
spending their days and nights sitting, standing, or walking; who are devoted to the practice of meditation,
intent on their own welfare by warding off the defilements— such monks, O Great King, are called the "guardians of the city" in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
But those monks, O Great King, who teach, cause others to teach, recite, cause others to recite, and explain the ninefold word of the Buddha— both in meaning, in phrasing, in method,
in reason, in cause, and in illustration— such monks, O Great King, are called "merchants of the Dhamma" in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
But those monks, O Great King, who are possessors and wealthy through the enjoyment of the jewel of the Dhamma, through the wealth of learning the scriptures and what has been heard,
who have penetrated the characteristics of the indicated meanings and syllables, who are wise and expansive— such monks, O Great King,
are called "the foremost merchants of the Dhamma" in the Blessed One’s city of the Dhamma.

But those monks, O Great King, who have penetrated the sublime teaching, who have mastered the analysis and exposition of objects, and who have reached the perfection of the virtues of training—such monks, O Great King, are called "renowned upholders of the Dhamma" in the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma.
Thus well-analyzed, O Great King, is the Blessed One’s City of Dhamma; thus well-constructed, thus well-ordered.
Thus well fulfilled, thus well established, thus well guarded, thus well protected, and thus difficult for adversaries and enemies to overcome—
for these reasons, O Great King, for this cause, by this method, and by this inference,
it should be known that the Blessed One exists.
"Just as, having seen a city,
well-arranged and delightful,
people know [its details] by inference,"
Just as one sees the greatness of a carpenter,
so too, having seen the excellent city of Dhamma belonging to the Lord of the World;
They know by means of inference that "the Blessed One exists";
they know by means of inference.
Having seen a wave in the ocean:
"As this wave is seen,
it will become very great."
Thus [I praise] the Buddha, the dispeller of sorrow,
the unconquered in all respects,
who has attained the destruction of craving.
It is the liberation from the cycle of existence.
It is to be known by inference,
even for those including the gods, upon seeing a wave.
Just as the spreading of smoke indicates fire,
so too will the Buddha be supreme;
they know this by means of inference.
Having seen the mountain rising high, [he thought]:
"Just as this one rises so high,
that Himavat will be even higher."
Having thus seen Dhammagiri,
cooled and free from acquisitions,
the lofty mountain of the Blessed One—
Immovable and well-established.
It is to be known by inference after having seen the mountain of Dhamma.
For thus that Great Hero shall become the foremost Buddha,
just like the king of elephants.
Having seen the footprint,
humans know by inference:
"This is a great elephant."
In the same way, having seen the footprint of the wise Buddha-elephant,
they know it by means of inference.
"He will be exalted.
They know this by inference,
having seen the terrified tortoise.
"Terrified by the sound of the king of beasts,
these young elephants flee;
even so it is when they see the followers of other sects."
When the mind is terrified by what is widespread,
it must be known through inference that the King of Dharma has roared.
Having seen the earth extinguished,
with its green foliage and great waters,
they know it by inference.
Just as [the fire] was extinguished by a great cloud,
so too, seeing these people filled with joy and delight, [he felt the same].
It is to be known through inference,
moistened by the cloud of Dhamma;
having seen the thick mud clinging [to it].
When the earth has reached the stage of the *kalala*,
they know by inference that a great mass of water has come to pass.
In the same way, seeing these people mired in the mud of passion,
being carried away by the river of the Dhamma, [I have crossed over].
Having seen this earth, together with its devas, immersed in the ocean of Dhamma and having reached the nectar of the Dhamma.
The great mass of Dhamma is to be known through inference;
they know it by means of inference.
Having smelled this supreme fragrance, [he knows]:
"Just as this scent blows forth,
so shall the trees come into bloom."
In the same way, this fragrance of virtue wafts through the world including the devas;
it is to be known by inference.
“There is a Buddha, unsurpassed.

Great King, it is possible to demonstrate the power of a Buddha by means of a hundred such reasons, a thousand reasons, a hundred causes, a thousand causes, a hundred methods, a thousand methods, a hundred similes, and a thousand similes.

Great King, it is just as when a skilled garland-maker, following the instructions of his teacher and through his own personal skill, creates a magnificent and variegated heap of garlands from a heap of various flowers.
In the same way, Great King, that Blessed One possesses infinite and immeasurable qualities like a heap of variegated flowers;
and I, now in the teaching of the Victor, like a garland-maker who strings flowers, shall illuminate the power of the Buddha through inference— by following the path of former teachers,
by the strength of my own intellect, and for incalculable reasons.
“But you, however, should generate the desire to hear on this matter.

“It is difficult, venerable Nāgasena, for others to demonstrate the power of a Buddha by such means as inference. I am satisfied, venerable Nāgasena, with your most wonderful exposition of the question.
The first question on inference.
